```{r global_options, include=FALSE}
# Necessary packages
packages_required <- c("dplyr", "divent", "doFuture", "progressr")

# Already installed?
packages_installed <- vapply(
  packages_required, 
  FUN = requireNamespace, 
  FUN.VALUE = TRUE, 
  quietly = TRUE
) 
# Install missing packages
install.packages(names(packages_installed)[!packages_installed])

# knitr options
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  cache = TRUE, 
  message = FALSE, 
  warning = FALSE
)

# Random seed
set.seed(97310)
```

Computer-intensive tasks can be run in parallel thanks to the **future** and **doFuture** [@Bengtsson2021] packages.

The following functions are concerned:

- `profile_hill()`
- `profile_similarity()`
- `accum_sp_tsallis()`
- `accum_sp_hill()`

# Progress bar

These functions can report their progress thanks to the **progressr** package.

The progress bar must be activated and its interface chosen.
Since all progress bars rely on package *cli* in divent, the "cli" handler is a good choice.

```{r}
#| eval: false
library("progressr")
handlers("cli", global = TRUE)
```

# Example

The diversity profile of example data is computed sequentially.
The computing time is measured.

```{r}
library("divent")
system.time(
  the_profile <- profile_hill(paracou_6_abd[1,], n_simulations = 100)
)
autoplot(the_profile)
```

# Parallel plan

It can be parallelized by setting a hardware strategy.
The following example launches several simultaneous copies of R on the local computer: it works on all operating systems.
The number of parallel processes here is the number of logical CPUs.

```{r}
library("doFuture")
plan(multisession, workers = availableCores())
```

The same computation is now run faster.

```{r}
system.time(
  the_profile <- profile_hill(paracou_6_abd[1,], n_simulations = 100)
)
```

The default strategy is `sequential`.
It should be restored.

```{r}
plan(sequential)
```

Other possible strategies are forking (`multicore`), unavailable on Windows, and `cluster`, on several computers.

See the documentation of the *future* package, namely `future::plan()`.

# Limits

Setting up the parallel code and gathering the results takes time so the performance of sequential simulations may be better if they are fast.
